Hey any advice on having a baby? What where you most scared off?

Hypothetically speaking....

HYPOTHETICALLY....

Hypothetically, congratulations!

I was most scared of being forced to have a cesarean, and of people doing stuff to my baby that I didn't agree to right after birth. I managed to avoid both despite ending up at the hospital instead of at home.

1st trimester was actually the hardest, the fatigue was incredible. Don't let her push herself too hard in the first trimester, the fatigue will lift in a few weeks. I pushed myself too hard because I was mad I felt useless and earned a miscarriage scare. The food aversions usually eventually go away after delivery. The mood swings are already happening I think, too, including bouts of rage. Knowing to expect it helped. A first pregnancy is a wild ride mentally, your brain is likely to look for and invent problems in the relationship and in general. Realize that's what's going on and don't listen to it.

Snacks are very important, for both nausea and because total energy/emotional crash is always just around the corner. Raw milk can help control nausea, but not pasteurized milk because the heat destroys the vitamin B6, I think it is. Eating gets easier after the 1st trimester, don't worry too much about diet yet if the nausea is bad.

2nd trimester is usually the fun one, energy is back, nausea goes away for most women, visible bump. If you want to plan a trip or something, this is the time. Snacks continue to be very important. Protein is important now, it can prevent preeclampsia. I started getting leg cramps toward the end, that's due to mineral need. Cal mag citrate liquid, bone grow, something like that to take shots of helps. Bone broth is obviously good, but this is an every day need. Otherwise it's all coming out of mama's bones and teeth. Vitamin K2 also very important. Staying hydrated is hard and important.

Consider a Bradley Method birthing class starting around this time, lots of info on all kinds of stuff in it. Very useful in preparing both parents, preventing complications, understanding what to expect in labor, and tools for pain management, exercises to prepare, etc.

3rd trimester the baby can hear now and remember sounds patterns and voices after birth. I drank a lot of kombucha and it really helped control the edema, which can get quite unpleasant. Wedge pillow for heartburn may be necessary. Again with snacking and hydration, protein and minerals. The baby can taste what the mother is eating through the amniotic fluid. You can get an object called a fetoscope and listen to the heartbeat at home for fun.

I didn't research breastfeeding as much as I should have beforehand, it is more learned than intuitive. You should find contact info for an IBCLC beforehand in case there is any breastfeeding difficulty and call right off the bat. Lesser LCs are useless. Clusterfeeding and the fact that breastfed babies have different weight gain patterns than bottle and formula fed babies are useful to know about.

I didn't write down a birth plan, it would have reduced the amount of talking I had to do. Talking in labor was the worst.

My husband's most important role in labor was counterpressure for pain management. Also, calling out the sex of the baby, and staying with him to protect him from potential rogue nurses.

I wish we'd done fewer ultrasounds. I wish I'd tried harder to eat and drink during early labor. I wish we'd sent someone for real food after the birth. I didn't really eat or sleep for like 3 days and I didn't realize I was doing it. I couldn't eat the unsalted hospital food.

Skin to skin after birth is great for both parents, good way for dads to bond their baby without feeding it, and helps mom's milk come in. We also did baby wearing with wraps or a ring sling, never lugged around a baby in a car seat or bought a stroller. In the beginning, Clammy had to wear him when we went anywhere because I needed postpartum physical therapy. Probably because I pushed myself too hard physically the whole pregnancy, but my midwife and OB thought the pain was normal and going to go away on its own after birth. The pain didn't really get me down, though, I was high AF on the hormones.

You can start elimination communication from birth if you want to. I started at 4 months because I felt nervous and overwhelmed before then, but I was just psyching myself out over nothing. Godiaperfree.com it's where I learned. There's a book you can buy, but there's also tons of free info and resources.

Wetness is what causes most diaper rash. Make sure the skin is dry before the diaper goes on. The baby wipes were the primary culprit for us, the moisture stays longer than plain water. If that's not it, it may be a digestive complaint.

Newborns don't know how to breathe yet, so they do it weird and take pauses, then gasp and that's normal. You'll still constantly check if they're breathing. Sleeping in the same room as mom and dad helps them learn to breathe.

All progress with babies is nonlinear. Baby is starting to sleep longer, maybe through the night even, then stops? Baby rolls once and won't do it again for 3 weeks? Baby says a word or does a sign language sign for a week and never again? That's just how they are, you didn't cause it, the baby is fine.
